title: How Do You Run a Church Meeting Worth Having?
subtitle: Most church meetings are where decisions go to die. A good one is rarer than a good sermon, and harder

sections.title: The Room Full of Fog
sections.body:
You have been in the meeting. Twelve people, two hours, no decision. Someone raised a concern that was really a grievance. Someone told a story that was really a campaign. The chairman lost the thread around minute forty and never found it again. Everyone left tired. Nothing was settled. And next month you will meet again to not settle it once more.

This is not an administrative failure. It is a spiritual one. A church that cannot decide cannot move, and a church that cannot move is already dying, it just has not noticed yet. The deacons who meet for two hours and decide nothing are not stewarding the church's time. They are spending it, and it is not their money.

We treat meetings as the unholy part of ministry, the price we pay for the holy parts. That is the lie. The meeting is where the body either acts as a body or reveals that it is not one. The fog in the room is not a scheduling problem. It is a discipleship problem with a calendar invitation attached.

sections.title: Why Most of Them Are Bad
sections.body:
Most church meetings are bad for reasons no one will say out loud. They are bad because no one decided beforehand what the meeting was for. They are bad because the agenda was a list of topics, not a list of decisions. They are bad because the pastor would rather be liked than clear, and so he lets the conversation wander rather than risk telling a beloved old saint that his point is not on the agenda.

A topic is not a decision. New building. Youth ministry. Parking. These are not items. These are weather systems. You can talk about parking until the Lord returns and never decide a single thing about it, and many committees have made a decade of doing exactly that.

And they are bad because we have confused process with prayerfulness. We think the longer we deliberate, the more spiritual we are being. Sometimes the longest deliberation is simply the deepest cowardice. We keep talking because to stop talking is to decide, and to decide is to be responsible, and responsibility is the thing the fog was protecting us from all along.

sections.title: What a Good Meeting Actually Does
sections.body:
A good meeting does one thing the bad meeting cannot. It ends with a decision and a name attached to it. Not a feeling. Not a consensus that evaporates in the parking lot. A decision, written down, with someone responsible for it and a date by which it is done.

The agenda for a good meeting is a list of verbs. Decide whether to hire. Approve the budget line. Choose between the two contractors. Each item is a fork in a road, and the meeting exists to walk the church down one side of it. If an item cannot be phrased as a decision to be made, it is not ready for the meeting, and putting it there only feeds the fog.

Good meetings are also short, because brevity is a form of respect. The volunteers in that room gave you their Tuesday night. They have children at home and jobs in the morning. A meeting that runs long because the leader could not steer is a meeting that taught those volunteers their time is worthless to you. They will remember that lesson. They will remember it the next time you ask them to serve.

sections.title: How to Lead the Decision Home
sections.body:
Before the meeting, write the decisions. Send them out. Let people pray and think and arrive ready, instead of meeting their own opinions for the first time in the room. The work that happens before the meeting is what determines whether the meeting is worth holding.

In the room, name the decision out loud and keep naming it. When the conversation drifts, and it will drift, pull it back gently and without apology. So we are deciding whether to hire. Bill, you have a concern. Is it about whether, or about who. Make the distinction. The distinction is the leadership.

Then close it. Call the question. Let the body act. And here is the part most leaders skip out of fear: write down who is responsible and when it is due, while everyone is still in the room to hear their name. A decision with no name attached is not a decision. It is a wish the committee agreed to have together, and it will be back on next month's agenda, exactly where it was, having aged but not moved.

sections.title: Stewards of Other People's Hours
sections.body:
The people in that room did not have to come. They came because they love the church, or at least because they used to, before the meetings taught them what love would cost in wasted evenings. Every hour you take from them is an hour they will not get back, and you are accountable for it the same way you are accountable for the offering.

We would never burn the building's money in the parking lot. We do something worse every month and call it governance. We burn the hours of faithful people who gave them freely, and we do it slowly, so no one notices the fire.

Lead the meeting like the time is holy, because it is. Decide the thing. Name the person. Close the door and let them go home to their families with the gift of an evening that meant something. A church that learns to meet well learns something larger than meetings. It learns that it can act. And a church that knows it can act is a church that is still alive.
